title: Canal discovered at ancient quarry in Egypt

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Archeologists working at an Aswan granite quarry where stones were cut have discovered a canal which they believe was used to help float some of ancient Egypt’s largest stone monuments to the river Nile. It has long been suspected that ancient workers moved these massive artifacts directly to their final destinations along waterways. Ancient artwork depicts Egyptians using rafts to move huge monuments like obelisks (tall, pointed columns) or statues, and canals have also been discovered at the Giza pyramids and the Luxor Temple. But the new-found canal, which has since been filled in, is the first proof discovered at a quarry in Aswan, in the south of Egypt. Almost all obelisks, including those at the Luxor and Karnak Temples, were originally cut in the Aswan area. This is very strong evidence that they may have loaded these stones into the canal at the quarry, according to Richard Parizek, a professor of geology at Penn State University in the US, who led the scientific tests proving the canal’s existence. It eliminates the need for a land connection, he explains.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: According to Adel Kelany, an inspector with Egypt’s Supreme Council of Antiquities who led the team that first dug up the site in 2002, larger obelisks can weigh more than 50 tons. A well-known unfinished obelisk at the quarry is thought to have weighed more than 1,100 tons. It was the largest such monument ever attempted but was abandoned after latent cracks emerged, revealing a rare glimpse of ancient construction practices. We have actually long suspected the existence of a canal linking the Nile to the quarry site, and it’s very nice to find this real confirmation, Salima Ikram, an Egyptologist at said the American University of Cairo.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Experts say the canal probably filled with water during the river Nile’s annual summer floods. Workers would have dragged the large stone columns onto rafts when the canal was dry and waited for them to float when the floods arrived and the water level rose. The canal was probably a natural split in the quarry granite, exploited and shaped by workers to make it more functional, the scientists add. Geologists found tooling marks along the canal similar to those where obelisks were removed.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Kelany and his team had been preparing the area for tourists in 2002 when they discovered a small trench in an otherwise flat area of solid rock. The workers suspected the trench fed into a main canal. The team was forced to halt digging when the excavation hit groundwater. They were unable to remove the water from the canal and if they had left it there, it would have become stagnant, providing ideal conditions for bacteria. ‘If we had left it like that, it would be quite dangerous as a tourist site,’ Kelany explains. Much of the site was therefore backfilled with gravel.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The site was left untouched until 2004, when a team of scientists set out to verify the canal’s existence through a series of tests that would replace the digging and so cause less damage to the site. The researchers used shallow seismic surveys to test for variations in the area’s topography by sending energy into the ground along lines that were at right angles to where the canal was thought to be. The team also tested the underground temperature, thinking the area of the canal depression would be cooler due to the presence of groundwater. The scientists were able to map about 456 feet (139 meters) of the canal but could not fully establish its extent because the site runs into a modern highway and an Islamic cemetery. However, they did establish that the site is roughly 1.2 miles (2 kilometers) from the Nile gorge, and scientists believe the canal becomes wider and deeper before possibly linking up with a main channel.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Along with finding the canal, archaeologists also turned up ancient graffiti on the rock which had been left behind by quarry workers, and also gridlines used in the obelisk-sculpting process. The depictions, which include images of dolphins and ostriches, are now endangered by rising water levels and an accumulation of salts, according to experts. Many sites in Egypt have been threatened by a build-up of salt since the building of the Aswan Dam, which prevents the Nile from flooding each year and washing away the minerals. ‘Generally, Egypt has always been salty because, of course, it used to be under the ocean,’ said Ikram, explaining that when the Aswan Dam was built the regular washing out of the salt from the land ceased and ‘destruction by salt’ became a problem in Egypt

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The problems at the original excavation site are magnified in part by the gravel used to fill it in. The gravel allows groundwater to rise to the level of the drawings which had been uncovered. Granite, a relatively non-porous rock, is not normally affected by water infiltration as much as other rocks like limestone. In this case, however, the capillary moisture is coming back out of the gravel since they backfilled the excavation, Parizek said. Scientists have proposed various solutions to stem the water flow. A clay barrier, for instance, could dam the previously excavated area and allow experts to pump out the existing water. ‘It’s just falling into ruin,’ Parizek said. There are artifacts there that are so unique that it would be a crime to lose them.
